title: Gerald McBoing-Boing
lede: UPA’s Oscar-winning short animated a Dr. Seuss story with flat, sparse drawings and limited movement, and set the look of mid-century “cartoon modern”.
summary: Animated short film by United Productions of America, directed by Robert Cannon, released by Columbia in 1950.

evidence.note: Based on the Wikipedia article and its quotation from The New York Times. No frames of the film were inspected for this record.

styles.note: The source of the style’s “limited animation” trait: flat shapes, few in-betweens, and sparse backgrounds.

context: Gerald McBoing-Boing is a 1950 animated short directed by Robert Cannon and produced by United Productions of America. Columbia Pictures released it on 4 November 1950. Phil Eastman and Bill Scott adapted a story by Dr. Seuss. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_McBoing-Boing).
It won the 1950 Academy Award for Best Animated Short. The Library of Congress selected it for the National Film Registry in 1995. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_McBoing-Boing).

Wikipedia quotes The New York Times: Cannon “was primarily responsible for the drawings, strongly reminiscent of a [Saul] Steinberg cartoon”, and Bill Hurtz and Herb Klynn did the design and the color. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerald_McBoing-Boing).
interpretation: UPA’s films moved studio animation away from rounded, fully animated characters toward flat, graphic drawing. That link between print illustration and motion is why the style record names limited animation as a trait.
borrow: Animate by moving, cutting, and swapping flat shapes rather than by smooth tweening, as the style’s motion facet describes.
next: Inspect frames from a licensed copy of the film and record what they show.
